title: Why Do We Get DÉJÀ VU? 🌀
description:
You open a strange door... and you've BEEN here before.

Déjà vu is not a memory, and it is not a glimpse of the future. The leading idea: a quick "that's familiar!" signal in your brain goes off by mistake (one trigger shown in the lab: a new room laid out just like one you have forgotten), your memory finds no record of the place, and the front of your brain spots that the two can't both be true. That clash is the eerie feeling: your brain catching its own mistake. Subscribe for a new strange question every day.

It can even feel like you know what happens next. When researchers tested that in virtual reality, people felt sure... and did no better than chance. About two in three people get déjà vu now and then, most often between about 15 and 25. (If it happens very often, or with blackouts or strange smells, tell a doctor.)
